2.add: The measured change is a calibration of the sensory map by visual experience, so the same acoustic timing cue comes to represent a different location.

3.add: Altering vision separately in central and peripheral regions tests which information guides calibration, since the auditory adjustments depended on which part of visual space remained available.

4.add: Optical displacement changes which timing value is appropriate for a mapped location, while the physical ITD delivered to the ears keeps its meaning as a time difference.

5.add: The lateral shell of the central nucleus and the external nucleus lie in the same midbrain complex but differ in plasticity, and the physiological comparison localized a major adaptive change to the transformation between the two representations.

third_paragraph.6: The experiment identifies ICX as a site that expresses adaptive plasticity. The opposite adaptive shifts in owls raised with leftward and rightward displacements link the measured timing change to the direction of the visual shift.

8.add: The comparison supports developmental regulation of auditory-map plasticity, with the juvenile owl adapting after 28 days and the adult showing little change after 183 days.

9.add: These measurements establish the temporal course of functional adaptation, and a changing best ITD can result from altered weighting of several inputs.

10.add: Acquisition of a new map and recovery of a previously established map are different experimental demands, and the communal aviary conditions defined the boundary of about 200 days.

11.add: The reversal supports experience-dependent selection of timing inputs, whether through new connections, altered synaptic strengths or changes in inhibition.

12.add: The oldest animal recovered when housed in the rich communal environment, so access to the normal calibration persisted into adulthood.

13.add: Recovery was observed in owls older than two years, whereas a large novel shift was strongly reduced when a displacement was first introduced late in life.

14.add: Flight, social interaction, attention and sensory richness differed between the cage and the aviary, so recovery depended on the environment in which the owls lived, and the age limit applied to the restricted cage conditions.

15.add: Transfer from cages to the aviary was sufficient for localization accuracy and tectal timing to recover in adults that had failed to recover in cages.

third_paragraph.16: Age and environment jointly influence the amount of adaptation that is expressed. Accounting for housing conditions turns an apparently universal biological deadline into a condition-dependent sensitive period.

18.add: The centrally instructed region changed more, so instruction acted regionally on the part of the map that received appropriate visual experience.

19.add: Peripheral and central representations can each be instructed by the visual experience of the corresponding region of visual space.

20.add: Topographic instruction means that each part of the map receives its own information about how it should change, whereas a global error signal would shift the whole map uniformly.

21.add: Drug sensitivity establishes a receptor contribution to that response, and the normal recordings supplied the baseline for interpreting learned responses.

22.add: Local application of AP-5 after the responses had developed tests their expression, and the tuning moved toward its normal component as the learned responses were reduced.

23.add: Experience changes the circuit properties that determine how different inputs generate spikes, and AP-5 sensitivity followed the learned side in both prism directions.

third_paragraph.24: CNQX therefore reduced normal and learned responses similarly, whereas AP-5 could reduce the learned side preferentially. Reducing non-NMDA depolarization can also reduce the voltage-dependent contribution of NMDA receptors, so the two receptor classes contribute together to the spike response.
third_paragraph.25: The established result is a differential dependence of the spike response on NMDA-receptor activation. Receptor number, receptor subunits and the NMDA-to-AMPA current ratio are mechanisms consistent with the observed pharmacology.
third_paragraph.26: The change is consistent with maturation of the circuit supporting learned responses. AP-5 still reduced auditory firing, so NMDA receptors continued to contribute, and what changed was the differential sensitivity between normal and learned inputs.
third_paragraph.27: The preferential effect on learned responses disappeared as age and days of prism experience increased together. A proposed increase in AMPA contribution, a decrease in NMDA contribution or altered inhibition are candidate explanations for the change, which tracks both chronological maturation and accumulated sensory experience.
third_paragraph.28: The distinctive pharmacology of learned responses is expressed downstream of the tested ICCls responses. AP-5 and CNQX reduced both flanks of ICCls tuning similarly, whereas AP-5 preferentially reduced learned responses in ICX.

29.add: Bicuculline acted on an existing circuit during the recording session, so the revealed response separates the available excitatory information from the timing information expressed in spikes when inhibition is active.

30.add: Adaptive excitation had already formed at this stage, and inhibition held part of it hidden from the spike tuning.

31.add: The inhibitory influence acted on learned timing values even when NMDA-receptor activation was reduced, so it is separable from the NMDA dependence of the response.

third_paragraph.32: The two pharmacological properties are separable. A site can show selective GABAergic suppression of learned timing inputs without a selective AP-5 effect, so differential inhibition is evaluated directly with bicuculline and not inferred from differential NMDA sensitivity.

33.add: Early inhibition masked learned inputs, whereas later inhibition suppressed the original normal inputs, so the same inhibitory system favored different timing values at different stages of adaptation.

34.add: Tracer anatomy therefore tests whether physiological map shifts are accompanied by structural remodeling of the pathway that carries timing input.

36.add: The direction of the extension corresponded to the direction of the physiological map shift, so the anatomical and physiological changes fit together.

37.add: Prism-reared adults therefore added axon to the adaptive region and did not merely retain juvenile axons.

38.add: Boutons are the presynaptic swellings at which transmitter release can occur, so bouton-bearing branches in the expanded region are potential sites of new input.

third_paragraph.39: These measures describe structural opportunities for auditory input in the adaptive portions of the projection. A larger anatomical projection can coexist with physiological suppression when inhibitory input or synaptic efficacy limits its expression.

40.add: Axons and boutons around the peak of the normal projection remained, so the anatomical substrate for normal timing inputs persisted alongside the adaptive inputs, and their physiological expression is regulated by synaptic strength and inhibition.

41.add: Hunting combined several features of experience, including live prey, movement, sound and consequences for errors, and the adult shift of about 25 µs was smaller than the juvenile response.

42.add: Under controlled stimulation the responses of individual sites agreed more consistently with the adaptive mapping after hunting than after prism experience alone.

43.add: Strike success covaried with the amount of adaptive timing-map shift, so neural tuning and behavioral outcome tracked each other during hunting experience.

third_paragraph.44: Attention, arousal, sensory information and reward are proposed contributors to the enhanced plasticity. The compound hunting experience increased adaptive plasticity in the adult map.
third_paragraph.45: Developmental age, prior calibration, environmental richness and behavioral engagement all affect the amount or form of plasticity expressed. Complementary evidence from regional manipulations, recordings, receptor blockade and tracing together supports an account in which visual information shapes the circuit that localizes sound.

inserts.title: The optic tectum aligns auditory and visual maps
paragraphs: The optic tectum is a midbrain structure that receives visual input and auditory space information. In the barn owl, a sound and a visible object at the same place normally drive neurons at the same tectal location.

Alignment of the two maps requires that each acoustic timing cue corresponds to the right place in visual space. Brainard and Knudsen tested this correspondence by displacing vision 23° horizontally with prisms in juvenile owls.

After prism rearing the auditory timing preference at a tectal site was appropriate for the displaced visual field and no longer for the original one. The auditory map moved to realign with vision. The tectal auditory and visual maps normally agree, and the prism experiment tests how that agreement is established.
notes: The tectum holds a visual map and an auditory map that normally agree.
Two maps.
A neural map places neighboring locations in tissue at neighboring stimulus locations.
The optic tectum contains an auditory map and a visual map.
Normal alignment.
A sound and a visible object at one location normally activate the same part of the tectum.
Prism rearing.
Juvenile owls wore prisms that displaced vision by 23 degrees horizontally.
Visual receptive fields were measured without the prisms to give the normal anatomical reference.
Result.
Neurons acquired auditory timing preferences appropriate for the displaced visual field.
Meaning.
Sounds did not move, and signals did not pass through the prisms.
The correspondence between timing cues and represented space changed.
Why alignment matters.
If the maps disagreed, a sound would draw the owl to a place that differs from the visible object that made it.
Alignment allows one command to point the head at both.
What the prisms test.
Prisms change the visual map relative to the world while leaving the acoustic cues alone.
A change in the auditory map therefore reflects recalibration.

inserts.title: Best ITD is the peak of a timing tuning curve
paragraphs: A tuning curve plots the response of a neuron against a stimulus parameter. Best ITD is the timing difference at the peak of the curve, and it is not the only value that can activate the neuron. Best ITD therefore summarizes where along the timing axis the response is largest.

Brainard and Knudsen compared best ITD with the position of the visual receptive field at tectal sites. In normal owls, best ITD changed systematically with visual azimuth, so each ear-leading value corresponded to a direction.

The normal relationship between best ITD and azimuth is the reference against which prism-induced shifts are measured. A shift of best ITD at a site with the same visual receptive field indicates a change in calibration.
notes: Best ITD summarizes where a timing tuning curve peaks, and it gives a way to compare sites and animals.
Tuning curve.
A tuning curve relates response to a controlled stimulus parameter.
Here the parameter is the interaural time difference in microseconds.
Best ITD.
Best ITD is the timing difference that produced the strongest response.
Other timing values can also activate the neuron.
Normal relation.
In normal owls best ITD changed systematically with visual azimuth.
Ear-leading labels indicate which ear receives the waveform first.
Reference for prisms.
A visual receptive field marks the location that the site represents.
A change of best ITD at a fixed visual location measures the shift in calibration.
Units.
Timing differences are measured in microseconds, and direction is measured in degrees.
Why not the only value.
A tuning curve has a width, so values near the peak also drive the neuron.
Best ITD marks the center of the response.
Using the relation.
Because best ITD changes systematically with azimuth in normal owls, a measured best ITD predicts which visual location the site represents.
Departures from the prediction measure calibration shifts.

inserts.title: ICCls and ICX are successive collicular stages
paragraphs: The lateral shell of the central nucleus, ICCls, provides timing-specific input to the external nucleus, ICX. ICX combines information across frequency channels and sends a spatially ordered auditory representation to the optic tectum. ICCls therefore precedes ICX in the pathway that reaches the tectum.

Brainard and Knudsen distinguished the two regions using anatomical reconstructions and response properties. Adaptation could alter their auditory responses differently, so recording location had to be known for each site.

In owls raised with a 23° visual displacement, ICX timing preferences shifted while ICCls timing representations remained normal. The change in calibration therefore occurs in the transformation from the first stage to the second. The first stage preserves the normal timing code, and the second stage expresses the adapted code.
notes: Two neighboring stages in the same midbrain complex behaved differently after prism rearing.
ICCls.
The lateral shell of the central nucleus contains frequency-organized representations with timing-specific output.
ICX.
The external nucleus combines information across frequency channels.
It supplies a spatially ordered auditory representation to the optic tectum.
Locating recordings.
Sites were assigned using anatomical reconstructions and response properties.
Result.
ICX timing preferences shifted after 23-degree prism rearing.
Upstream timing representations remained normal.
Meaning.
Proximity in the tissue does not imply identical plasticity.
The adaptive change was localized to the transformation between the two stages.
Two measurements.
Anatomical reconstructions and response properties identified each recording region.
Both were needed because the regions neighbor one another.
Where plasticity appears.
A change that appears in ICX and is absent in ICCls implies that the first stage still supplies a normal timing code.
The adaptation must therefore occur in how ICX uses that code.

inserts.title: A sensitive period is a window of heightened plasticity
paragraphs: A sensitive period is an age range during which a particular experience can alter a circuit especially strongly. Outside the window, the same experience produces little change. Sensitive periods are defined by comparing animals of different ages that receive the same experience.

Brainard and Knudsen compared the response to 23° prisms in juvenile and adult barn owls, measuring preferred ITD against visual receptive-field locations. An owl fitted at 88 days of age showed a substantial adaptive shift after 28 days.

An adult fitted after one year of age showed much less change even after 183 days. The same sensory mismatch and the same neural response measure produced different results at the two ages. The comparison isolates age as the variable that changes the outcome.
notes: Age determines how much the auditory map can change in response to the same visual displacement.
Definition.
A sensitive period is an age range of especially strong plasticity for a given experience.
Comparison.
Juvenile and adult barn owls received the same 23-degree prisms.
Preferred ITD was measured against visual receptive-field location.
Juvenile owl.
An owl fitted at 88 days showed a substantial adaptive shift after 28 days.
Adult owl.
An adult fitted after one year of age showed much less change after 183 days.
Longer exposure did not compensate for older age.
Meaning.
Auditory-map plasticity is regulated by development.
Same mismatch.
Every owl received a 23-degree displacement, so differences in outcome belong to age and not to the size of the visual error.
Reading the numbers.
The juvenile owl adapted substantially in 28 days, and the adult showed much less change in 183 days.
Time under prisms was not the limiting factor.

inserts.title: Chronic recording follows the same preparation over time
paragraphs: Chronic recording means returning to a recording preparation across days and weeks. The map of a single animal can be measured before and during adaptation. Repeated measurement distinguishes a stable preexisting map from one that changes during experience.

Brainard and Knudsen followed tectal timing preferences with chronic electrodes or by sampling multiple sites across successive sessions after prisms were attached. With 23° prisms the full adaptive change was about 57 µs.

Younger owls progressed toward that value over days and weeks, whereas older owls often remained near the normal reference. Time courses differed across ages and individuals and did not follow one universal rate. Rates of adaptation therefore vary with the age and history of each owl.
notes: A map can only be shown to change if it is measured repeatedly.
Chronic recording.
The recording preparation is revisited over time, so each animal serves as its own baseline.
Expected change.
With 23-degree prisms the full adaptive change in best ITD was approximately 57 microseconds.
Younger owls.
They progressed toward the full shift over days and weeks.
Older owls.
They often remained near the normal reference.
Variability.
Time courses differed across ages and individuals.
A changing best ITD can reflect altered weighting of several inputs.
Time courses.
Some owls changed over days and others over weeks.
Older owls often stayed near the normal reference.
Population sampling.
Repeated sampling of tectal sites tracks the map as a population and does not follow one synapse.
A changing best ITD can come from new weighting of several inputs.
Why 57 microseconds.
The value is the expected full change for a 23-degree displacement, so a shift can be read as a fraction of complete adaptation.
Progress toward it measures how far the map has adapted.

inserts.title: Recovery restores a previously calibrated map
paragraphs: Recovery is a return to a cue-to-location relationship that the animal established earlier. It differs from acquiring a new displacement, which requires an unfamiliar mapping. The shifted map just before prism removal provided the comparison for recovery.

Brainard and Knudsen removed prisms and followed preferred ITDs with chronic tectal recordings. Owls whose prisms were removed at 108, 238 and 1,208 days of age recovered normal tuning over a period of normal vision.

Recovery occurred in the oldest animal when it lived in the rich communal environment. An adult circuit can therefore retain access to a normal calibration that it does not express while the prisms are worn. Recovery shows that the normal mapping remains available as an alternative state of the same circuit.
notes: Returning to a familiar mapping is easier for an adult circuit than acquiring a new one.
Recovery and acquisition.
Recovery returns to a mapping that was established before.
Acquisition requires an unfamiliar displacement.
Procedure.
Prisms were removed, and preferred ITDs were followed with chronic tectal recordings.
The shifted map just before removal gave the comparison.
Ages.
Prisms were removed at 108, 238 and 1,208 days of age.
All owls recovered normal tuning during normal vision.
Environment.
Recovery occurred even in the oldest animal when it lived in the communal environment.
Meaning.
A normal calibration remains accessible in adults.
Why recovery is informative.
If adult circuits lost the normal mapping, removing prisms would leave the shifted map in place.
Return to normal tuning shows that the mapping was retained.
Rich environment.
The oldest owl lived in a communal aviary.
Its recovery depended on that environment, as later experiments on housing show.

inserts.title: An instructive signal specifies the direction of change
paragraphs: An instructive signal carries information about how a representation should change, not only that a change is needed. A topographic instructive signal specifies the change separately for each location in the map. The distinction matters because the two possibilities make different predictions about where in the map changes occur.

Hyde and Knudsen adapted owls to leftward 23° prisms and then gave normal vision centrally while the peripheral field beyond 15° was occluded. After 11 days, central tectal timing moved toward normal while the occluded peripheral representation changed much less.

Different regions adjusted differently within the same animal. Visual information therefore contributes to calibration point by point and is not a single signal derived from where the owl directs its gaze.
notes: The experiment asks what kind of visual information instructs the auditory map.
Instructive signal.
An instructive signal specifies the direction of change in addition to signaling error.
A topographic signal does so separately for each location.
Alternative.
Instruction could depend only on whether an orienting movement ended at the correct central visual position.
Manipulation.
After adaptation to leftward prisms, normal vision was given centrally while the periphery beyond 15 degrees was occluded.
Result.
After 11 days central tectal timing moved toward normal.
The occluded peripheral representation changed much less.
Meaning.
A signal derived only from central gaze would predict a more uniform change.
Two hypotheses.
One hypothesis ties instruction to the correctness of an orienting movement toward the center of gaze.
The other supplies instruction separately for each region of the map.
Comparison within an animal.
Central and peripheral representations were compared in the same owl, so both regions shared the same age, history and environment.

inserts.title: NMDA and non-NMDA receptors are glutamate-gated channels
paragraphs: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in these collicular circuits. NMDA and non-NMDA receptors are two classes of glutamate-activated ion channel, and each class can be blocked with a selective antagonist. Antagonists block receptor activation without removing the receptors.

Feldman and Knudsen applied AP-5 to antagonize NMDA receptors and CNQX to antagonize non-NMDA receptors near a recording site. In normal ICCls and ICX recordings, both drugs reduced auditory responses. The antagonists were ejected near the recorded neurons with small currents.

Control and recovery measurements checked that the change followed reversible local drug application. The reduction by each antagonist measures the contribution of that receptor class to the spike response. A reduction of firing therefore indicates that the receptor class contributes to expressing the response.
notes: Receptor antagonists reveal which kind of glutamate receptor supports a response.
Glutamate.
Glutamate is the excitatory transmitter considered in these experiments.
Two classes.
NMDA receptors are blocked by AP-5.
Non-NMDA receptors are blocked by CNQX.
Local application.
Drugs were applied near a recording site, so the effect remains local to the recorded neurons.
Normal responses.
In normal ICCls and ICX recordings both drugs reduced auditory responses.
These recordings supplied the baseline for interpreting learned responses.
Controls.
Control and recovery periods checked that the effect was reversible.
Receptor classes.
NMDA receptors and non-NMDA receptors respond to the same transmitter but can contribute differently to a response.
Selective antagonists separate their contributions.
Baseline for later slides.
Normal ICCls and ICX responses depended on both classes.
Differences in later experiments are interpreted against this baseline.
Selective antagonists.
AP-5 blocks the activation of NMDA receptors, and CNQX blocks non-NMDA receptors.
A drug that reduces firing identifies a receptor class that contributes to the response.
Reversibility.
Responses returned toward their original size after the drug was removed, which links the effect to the local application.

inserts.title: NMDA currents depend on the membrane voltage
paragraphs: NMDA-receptor currents depend on receptor activation and on the electrical state of the postsynaptic membrane. Depolarization makes the membrane voltage less negative and can increase the contribution of NMDA currents to excitation. The voltage dependence makes the effect of AP-5 a measure of NMDA contribution under the voltage reached during the response.

Feldman and Knudsen found greater AP-5 sensitivity of newly learned ICX responses than of normal responses during 30 to 154 days of prism experience. Their interpretation allowed changes intrinsic to the synapse and changes in the circuit that altered the voltage of the neuron during a response.
AP-5 sensitivity therefore reflects the synapse and the state of the neuron around it. Non-NMDA depolarization can raise the NMDA contribution, so the two receptor classes interact.
notes: The size of an NMDA contribution depends on the membrane voltage as well as on the synapse.
Voltage dependence.
NMDA currents depend on receptor activation and on the electrical state of the membrane.
Depolarization can increase the NMDA contribution.
Observed pharmacology.
Newly learned ICX responses were more sensitive to AP-5 than normal responses.
The experience ranged from 30 to 154 days.
Two readings.
A change intrinsic to the synapse could produce the sensitivity.
A change in the surrounding circuit that alters the voltage during a response could also produce it.
Interacting receptors.
Reducing non-NMDA depolarization can reduce the NMDA contribution.
Measurement.
The recordings captured spikes, so receptor numbers and subunits were not measured directly.
Why membrane state matters.
The same synaptic input can produce a different NMDA current when the membrane is more or less depolarized.
An altered circuit can change the voltage reached during a response.
What was and was not measured.
The experiments recorded spikes extracellularly.
They did not measure receptor subunits or the ratio of NMDA to AMPA current.

inserts.title: Disinhibition reveals hidden excitatory input
paragraphs: Disinhibition is the removal of inhibition, which can reveal excitation that the inhibition was suppressing. GABA mediates inhibition in the ICX experiments of Zheng and Knudsen, and bicuculline blocks GABA-A receptors. Excitation and inhibition converge on the same neuron, so the spike output reflects their balance.

In a normal owl, bicuculline increased responses while leaving the weighted timing preference approximately unchanged. During early prism adaptation, the same manipulation could shift the response toward learned ITDs.

Control, drug and recovery periods linked the changes to reversible local application. A response revealed by disinhibition was already supported by excitatory input, which inhibition had kept from appearing in the spikes. The balance between the two sets which timing values appear in the spike tuning.
notes: Blocking inhibition shows how much excitation is present but not expressed.
Disinhibition.
Removing inhibition can reveal excitation that was suppressed.
Pharmacology.
GABA is the inhibitory transmitter, and bicuculline blocks GABA-A receptors.
Normal owl.
Bicuculline increased responses.
The weighted timing preference stayed approximately the same.
Early adaptation.
The same drug shifted the response toward learned ITDs.
Meaning.
Excitatory input for the learned timing existed already.
Inhibition limited what the spikes expressed.
Why block inhibition.
Spikes show only the net result of excitation and inhibition.
Blocking GABA-A receptors reveals the excitation underneath.
Timing preference.
The weighted timing preference summarizes the whole tuning curve.
Its shift under bicuculline shows which inputs inhibition had been suppressing.
Recovery and control.
Control, drug and recovery periods were compared in the same recording.
A return toward baseline shows that the change followed the local drug application.
Interpretation.
The response revealed during early adaptation shows that excitatory input for learned timing already existed.
The excitation was suppressed by inhibition at that stage.

inserts.title: Anterograde tracing follows axons to their targets
paragraphs: Anterograde tracing labels projections from neuronal cell bodies toward their axon terminals. A tracer injected at one site fills the axons that leave it and shows where they end. The tracer is transported along the axons from the injection site to the terminals.

DeBello and colleagues injected biocytin into timing-defined ICC sites and reconstructed the labeled axons extending into ICX. A calcium-binding-protein stain identified the ICC core as an anatomical reference. The projection field is the region of ICX that contains the labeled terminals.

The labeling revealed the projection field and individual bouton-bearing axons. Anatomy separates a change in projection geometry from a change in physiological weighting alone. Quantifying axon length and boutons in the field gives a structural measure of the pathway.
notes: Tracing measures the structure of the pathway that carries timing input.
Anterograde tracing.
A tracer labels the projections that leave the injected cells and reach their terminals.
Injection sites.
Biocytin was injected into ICC sites with defined timing preferences.
Reconstruction.
Labeled axons extending into ICX were reconstructed.
A calcium-binding-protein stain marked the ICC core.
What was visible.
The projection field and individual axons with boutons were visible.
Scale bars of 500 and 100 micrometers accompany the published sections.
Use.
The anatomy distinguishes geometry from physiological weighting.
Reference stain.
The calcium-binding-protein stain marks the ICC core and provides landmarks for comparing animals.
Scale.
The published sections include scale bars of 500 micrometers for anatomical organization and 100 micrometers for the higher-magnification projection image.
Question addressed.
The anatomy asks whether the physiological map shift is accompanied by a structural change in the pathway.
Why anatomy complements physiology.
Spikes show what a neuron expresses.
Axons and boutons show the structure that supplies the input.
Timing-defined sites.
The injected ICC sites were defined by their timing preference, so the labeled axons can be related to the timing that the sites represent.

inserts.title: Boutons mark potential presynaptic contacts
paragraphs: A bouton is a swelling along an axon at which synaptic contacts can form. An additional branch is more relevant to circuit function when it carries boutons. Counting boutons therefore estimates the number of potential contacts.

DeBello and colleagues examined labeled axons in the adaptive flank and at the peak of the normal ICC-to-ICX projection. The prism-associated axons were branched and carried boutons, and bouton-bearing axons were present in both the newly expanded region and the normal region.

Boutons in the expanded region link altered projection geometry with potential presynaptic input. The sites of transmitter release in the adaptive region therefore added to those of the normal projection. Light microscopy resolves the swellings along each labeled axon.
notes: Branches matter for circuit function when they bear boutons.
Bouton.
A bouton is a swelling at which an axon can make a synaptic contact.
Regions examined.
The adaptive flank and the peak of the normal projection were examined.
Observation.
Prism-associated axons were branched and carried boutons.
Bouton-bearing axons were present in the newly expanded region and in the normal region.
Image detail.
The micrographs retain a 20-micrometer scale bar.
Meaning.
The anatomy supplies potential sites for new synaptic input in the adaptive region.
Adaptive flank and peak.
The adaptive flank is the part of ICX where prism-reared owls had extra projection.
The peak is the center of the normal projection.
Count of contacts.
Bouton number and axon density estimate potential contacts.
Their strength and efficacy need physiological measurement.
Image detail.
The original micrographs retain a 20-micrometer scale bar.
Expanded and normal regions.
Bouton-bearing axons appeared in the expanded region as well as in the normal projection region, which links a change in geometry to potential presynaptic input.

inserts.title: Hunting couples sound, vision and consequence
paragraphs: Hunting combines moving live prey, sounds made by the prey, visual information about its position and an immediate consequence for an inaccurate strike. Bergan and colleagues asked whether this behavior increases adult auditory plasticity.

Adult owls wore 17° prisms and received either dead mice or live mice during one-hour daily sessions in communal aviaries. After 10 weeks without hunting the median map shift was about 5 µs, and with hunting it was about 25 µs.

A separate group introduced directly to hunting showed a similar 26 µs shift after eight weeks. The behavior therefore increased adaptation in adults, and the larger shift was not explained by prior prism exposure alone.
notes: A natural behavior was added to the prism experience of adult owls.
Hunting features.
Live prey provide movement and rustling sounds, coupled visual and auditory information, and a consequence for inaccurate strikes.
Groups.
Adult owls wore 17-degree prisms.
They received dead mice or hunted live mice in one-hour daily sessions.
Shifts.
Without hunting the median shift after 10 weeks was about 5 microseconds.
With hunting it was about 25 microseconds.
Control group.
A separate group introduced directly to hunting showed a median shift of 26 microseconds after eight weeks.
Meaning.
Hunting increased adult map plasticity.
Prism size.
The prisms displaced vision by 17 degrees, smaller than the 23 degrees used in the juvenile experiments.
Housing.
Both groups lived in communal aviaries and had one-hour feeding sessions, so only the demand to capture live prey differed.
Question asked.
The study tested whether a behavior with ecological importance could raise adult plasticity above the level seen with prism wearing alone.
Interpretation of the groups.
Introducing a separate group directly to hunting reduced concern that earlier prism exposure explained the larger shift.

inserts.title: Strike success measures behavioral accuracy
paragraphs: Strike success is the proportion of attempts in which the owl captures the target mouse. It provides a behavioral outcome that can be compared with the neural map shift in the same animals. It is a direct measure of how well the owl uses its map.

Average success was about 89% without prisms and about 27% immediately after prism attachment. During hunting experience, improved capture performance covaried with the amount of adaptive timing-map shift.

A prism displaces the visual location of the prey relative to its sound, so accurate strikes require the auditory and visual estimates of position to agree. Recovery of strike success accompanies realignment of the auditory map. Better strikes therefore indicate a better match between where the owl hears and sees the prey.
notes: Behavior and neural tuning were measured together in the same experiment.
Strike success.
Strike success is the proportion of attempts in which the owl captures the mouse.
Effect of prisms.
Average success was about 89 percent without prisms.
It fell to about 27 percent immediately after prism attachment.
Why prisms impair hunting.
The prism shifts the apparent visual position of the prey, and the sound of the prey indicates a different position.
Improvement.
During hunting, improved capture performance covaried with the amount of adaptive timing-map shift.
Meaning.
Neural tuning and behavior are related outcomes of recalibration.
Experimental logic.
The owl hunts live mice, so each strike is a test of whether sound and vision agree.
Strike success is the behavioral readout.
Link to neurons.
The amount of timing-map shift measured in the tectum was related to improvement in capture.
Why success falls.
With prisms attached, an owl aims at the visual position of the mouse while the sound of the mouse indicates a different position.
Strikes miss until the maps realign.
Behavioral consequence.
Capture of live prey has a clear consequence, which makes strike success a meaningful measure of accuracy.
